# 4. Restorative Functions {#sec-functions}

Zone and position tell you where a project sits. Neither tells you what the land was actually made to do — and for a document with *restorative* in its title, that is the question. **Restorative functions** are the answer: five things a site can be designed to provide.

- **Water** (§4.1) — what soaks in, what runs off, and what the aquifer gets back
- **Soil and carbon** (§4.2) — what builds back up underneath
- **Habitat** (§4.3) — what can live there
- **Microclimate** (§4.4) — shade, temperature, and moisture right at the ground
- **Community and economy** (§4.5) — what the people hosting it actually get

**Functions are not positions.** A site does not pick one function the way it occupies one position. It delivers several at once, in varying amounts, and it can deliver them from almost anywhere on the two axes. This matters because some terms get used as though they named a position when they name a function. *Pollinator habitat* is treated as a spot on the sharing–sparing axis, but it is reachable under grazing (S2), on an ordinary converted parcel (S3), and on spared or retired ground (S4–S5) alike. *Native grassland* is the same. Keep the two apart and the confusion goes away: positions are **rows**, functions are **columns**, and a real project fills in several columns rather than sitting in one.

That grid is the natural companion to the [Levers × Scale-Zones matrix](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix) in §3.4 — one shows what a project can deliver, the other what a designer can reach for. It reflects the working-landscapes view: a mosaic of positions can carry many functions at once instead of trading them off wholesale (Kremen 2015; Grass et al. 2019 — *trace before citing*). The columns are defined here. Filling in every cell with a score is deliberately not attempted (§8, issue 6).

**A palette, not a scorecard.** Nothing here says a good project maximizes every column. Most sites can deliver a few. Some functions work against each other, and against generation, cost, and farming. What a site can reach depends on where it is and how it is built — the same conditionality §2.2 applies to full sharing. This says what is *reachable* on a given site, not what is *owed* by it.

**Four are about the land; one is about people.** Water, soil, habitat, and microclimate are things the ground does. Community and economy is what the project does for the people hosting it (§4.5). All five are *outcomes*, which is what separates them from the [pressures and levers](3-design-pressures.qmd): a pressure is a force pushing for something, a lever is a tool that acts, and a function is the result they can produce. [Social license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) is the pressure; [community benefit](5-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) and [screening](5-terminology.qmd#term-screening) are levers; the community actually being better off is the function they aim at. The same split appears in the [SCALE footprint](#sec-scale) below: the four land functions are its **Landscapes** domain (with parts of **Agriculture**), the fifth is **Communities**, and **Energy** is carried by the design pressures.

**Others are working on the same ground.** In ecosystem-services language, the four land functions are mostly *regulating and supporting services* — water regulation, soil formation, habitat — which keeps that literature within reach without adopting its habit of putting dollar figures on nature. NREL and DOE's **InSPIRE** program describes much the same posture from the operations side, as *low-impact solar development* [@macknick2022]. The names used here are kept independent of position deliberately, so a function can be claimed — and checked — whatever a site's zone or sharing position.

Each function below is set out the same way: how it works, what it depends on, where it is easiest and hardest to get, and how good the evidence is, following the verified / *trace-before-citing* discipline of the [Sources](sources.qmd).

---

### The SCALE footprint {#sec-scale}

SCALE reads a project across four domains at once — **Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy** — with each one running from restoring the land to using it up. The domains line up with the rest of this document: **Communities** ≈ the [community & economic function](#sec-fn-community) (with the [social-license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) pressure and [community-benefit](5-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) lever behind it); **Landscapes** ≈ the biophysical restorative functions in this chapter (water, ecosystems); **Energy** ≈ the [design pressures](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (cost, security); **Agriculture** ≈ agricultural continuity and the sharing–sparing axis (food security, marginality). SCALE judges, and is used here to judge: the reading says whether a project regenerates or depletes in each domain. What it does not do is draw a line. SCALE's own "limit of sustainability" implies a line a project either clears or does not, and whether this vocabulary should carry such a line, and on what measurements, is the open metrics question (§8, issue 5). The domains carry direction and judgment; they do not carry a pass mark.

![The SCALE footprint: a project's influence read across four domains (Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, Energy) and their sub-axes, each running from regeneration at the center to depletion at the rim. The reading is evaluative by design — that is what *restorative* commits the document to — but it is a direction of travel rather than a pass mark; no threshold line is drawn (§8, issue 5). The polygon shown is a worked example.](../figures/fig_scale_footprint.svg){#fig-scale}

### 4.1 Hydrologic function {#sec-fn-hydrologic}

**Mechanism.** An array reshapes the site water balance. Panels intercept rainfall and redistribute it — concentrating flow along drip lines at panel edges while sheltering the ground beneath — which alters the partition between infiltration, runoff, and evaporation. Shade lowers soil-surface evaporation and plant transpiration, so soil moisture is generally retained; altered cover and compaction change infiltration capacity; and the net effect on deep percolation, groundwater recharge, and stormwater runoff depends on how the ground layer and grading are designed. Restorative hydrologic design uses the array and its ground layer deliberately — to raise infiltration and recharge, to slow and filter runoff (reducing erosion and nutrient export), and to buffer soil moisture through dry spells. At a larger scale the array can change the water *budget*, not just the on-site balance: where solar displaces irrigated cropland it retires that field's consumptive use and saves groundwater at the basin scale [@stid2022; @stid2025] — the demand-side logic of [water-sustainability solar](6-archetypes.qmd#arch-water) (§6). That saving holds only where groundwater governance keeps it from being pumped elsewhere [@zwickle2021].

**Design dependencies.** Ground-layer composition is primary — deep-rooted perennial cover infiltrates where bare or gravel ground sheds. Panel and row geometry set where drip concentrates; grading and the placement logic of [solar prairie strips](6-archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) (siting along hydrologic features) put infiltration where runoff collects; the operational regime and the choice of ground cover carry the rest. The instrument migrates along the transect exactly as the [restoration modes](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) do — siting-led along hydrologic features at A2–A3, management-led through ground cover at A4–A5.

**Where on the map.** Broadly available, because water moves through every site — but most *legible* where the ground layer is designed for it (S2–S5: grazing, prairie/buffer, restored marginal and retired ground) and least so under bare-ground or gravel management. Solar prairie strips are its characteristic siting-led case; managed perennial cover is its characteristic case at scale.

**Evidence status.** The microclimate-to-soil-moisture link is **verified**: panel shade raises soil moisture and cuts evaporative and transpiration losses in drylands [@barrongafford2019], semi-arid grassland arrays show measurable aridity mitigation [@sturchio2025], water is the primary ecological variable in a water-limited framing of ecovoltaics [@knapp2024], and soil-moisture retention is documented in desert array interspaces [@pinos2026]. The size of the effect is bounded, though: at one semi-arid grassland array the carbon and water cycles barely changed [@kannenberg2023]. The *infiltration / recharge / stormwater-runoff* side — how panel drip and altered cover reshape the water balance at depth and at the plot-to-watershed scale — is **thinner**: a solar-hydrology review gathers what exists and offers stormwater guidance [@yavari2022], but the field evidence behind it is sparse. This is an active research frontier, and exactly what current field instrumentation is built to close: measured panel drip and runoff, soil-moisture profiles, and coupled surface–groundwater modeling. In short: the microclimate side is well-evidenced; the water-balance side is still a research frontier.

---

### 4.2 Soil & carbon function {#sec-fn-soil}

**Mechanism.** The array changes what the soil is asked to do. Where perennial, low-disturbance cover replaces a tilled row-crop baseline, roots stay in the ground year-round, traffic and tillage fall away, and soil organic carbon and aggregate stability can build back — the standard perennialization pathway, here running under and between the panels. The array's own shade and reduced evaporative demand alter the decomposition and moisture regimes that govern how fast carbon accumulates or turns over. Restorative soil design treats the ground layer as the working surface: perennial establishment, minimal disturbance, and a management regime that keeps cover continuous rather than resetting it. Construction cuts the other way — grading, trenching, and compaction during installation strip and disturb soil, so the early ledger can show a loss before it shows a gain.

**Design dependencies.** Ground-layer composition and establishment method are primary — deep-rooted perennial or native mix under no-till builds where an annual, tilled understory does not. Grazing regime and stocking density set whether animal return of nutrients and trampling help or compact; construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline decide how much of the starting soil is lost to the build. As with the hydrologic function, the instrument is siting-led early on the transect (which ground is disturbed, and how) and management-led at scale (the ground cover and grazing regime carried over years). The gains are slow and cumulative, so the operational regime — sustained, not one-time — carries most of the outcome.

**Where on the map.** Most reachable under perennial and grazed cover and native-grassland restoration (S2–S3), where the ground layer is designed for continuity, and on restored marginal or retired ground (S4–S5) recovering from a degraded baseline. Least available under annual tillage inside full-sharing cropping (S1) or wherever disturbance is frequent, since each reset spends the accumulated carbon. Regenerative solar grazing and solar prairie strips are its characteristic cases; the marginal-land-solar case depends on how degraded the starting soil was.

**Evidence status.** Early soil-carbon and soil-surface gains are **verified** for early-stage ecovoltaic grassland restoration [@krasner2025] — but the same evidence carries the caveats plainly: outcomes are **time-dependent**, the trajectory can start with construction-disturbance losses before it turns positive, and the magnitude is site-conditional on the starting baseline and climate. Longer-term accrual — whether early gains persist and deepen over the array's decades — is **thinner and largely trace**, a frontier rather than a settled number; direct long-run measurements at solar farms are scarce [@carvalho2024]. In short: the soil function is real and early-evidenced, but the multi-decade curve is still open.

### 4.3 Biodiversity & habitat function {#sec-fn-biodiversity}

*Pollinator habitat* and *native grassland* belong here: both are functions, reachable across S2–S5, rather than positions of their own on the sharing–sparing axis.

**Mechanism.** Habitat is built from the ground layer up. Floral plantings supply nectar and pollen; the vegetation's vertical and horizontal structure supplies nesting substrate, cover, and the heterogeneity that lets many species partition a single site — so pollinators, ground-nesting arthropods, and grassland birds find resources an annual monoculture does not offer. Panel shade also shifts the timing: partial shading delays bloom and increases late-season floral abundance [@graham2021]. The array furniture adds its own structure, and the management regime that keeps the planting diverse and undisturbed does as much as the seed mix. Restorative habitat design uses the interrows and array margins as the working habitat, not incidental green space.

**Design dependencies.** Seed-mix composition sets the ceiling — a native, floral-rich mix reaches species a turf understory cannot. Mowing and grazing *timing* is decisive, not merely their presence: disturbance during nesting or bloom undoes the resource it was meant to provide, so the operational calendar is a design lever in its own right [@blaydes2022]. Fragmentation geometry and the [influence-zone](5-terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) edge matter — several small arrays scattered through a landscape connect and edge differently than a few large ones, and edge-to-area ratio shapes which species the site reaches. As with the other functions, the instrument is siting-led where placement stitches into existing corridors and management-led where the ground cover and its calendar carry the habitat over years.

**Where on the map.** Obtainable from the productive middle right through the removal end (S2–S5) — wildflower interrows over grazing (S2), dedicated habitat plantings on converted ground (S3), and restored or retired parcels (S4–S5) — which is exactly why it reads as a function reachable at many positions rather than one. Least available under bare-ground, gravel, or intensively disturbed understories. Solar prairie strips and regenerative solar grazing are its characteristic cases.

**Evidence status.** **Verified** for grassland-bird gains at solar sites [@walston2025], for insect-community response to habitat establishment [@walston2024], and for bee-species diversity in pollinator-planted arrays [@bruningasocolar2025]. Pollinator-friendly solar scorecards codify these choices as scored attributes, though what each program credits differs [@epri2021]. But the finding is **context-dependent**, and the honest reading says so: the marginal habitat benefit is greatest where the surrounding landscape is already sparse in semi-natural habitat, and correspondingly smaller where semi-natural habitat is abundant. It is a real gain, not a uniform good — its size is set by what the site would otherwise have been, not by the planting alone.

### 4.4 Microclimate & thermal–water buffering function {#sec-fn-microclimate}

**Mechanism.** The array rewrites the near-surface energy balance. Panels intercept and redistribute incoming radiation, so daytime soil and canopy temperatures fall in their shade, longwave sheltering raises nighttime minima, and the vapor-pressure deficit under the array drops — the microenvironment swings less far in both directions across the day. That buffering couples tightly to the [hydrologic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-hydrologic): the same shade that cuts thermal extremes also cuts evaporative demand, so moisture is retained and the two functions rise and fall together. Restorative microclimate design tunes the geometry so the shelter lands where a heat- or water-stressed ground layer needs it, without starving it of the light it still requires.

**Design dependencies.** Module geometry and mounting height, row spacing and ground-coverage ratio, and tracking schedule set how much radiation is redistributed and where the shade falls through the day. For crops, the shade-tolerance match is decisive — the buffering is a benefit only where the ground layer can trade light for relief, and a cost where it cannot. The effect is inseparable from scale and array geometry: the same panels that shelter a dryland understory can over-shade a light-limited one, which is why this function turns on the design tipping-point rather than existing uniformly. The instrument is geometry-led throughout, and its sign flips with climate and crop.

**Where on the map.** Pronounced in hot, water-limited settings and for shade-tolerant ground layers, where lowered temperature and vapor-pressure deficit relieve real stress; muted to adverse in cool or humid settings and for light-demanding crops, where the shade subtracts more than it buffers. It is itself scale- and geometry-dependent — the [design tipping-point noted in §1.1](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) — so its availability is set by the array's form and the site's climate together, not by position on the sharing–sparing axis alone.

**Evidence status.** **Verified** for the underlying principles and for dryland effects: agrivoltaic and ecovoltaic microclimates redistribute radiation and buffer temperature and moisture [@sturchio2023; @sturchio2025], and soil-moisture and thermal moderation are documented in desert array interspaces [@pinos2026], with the foundational dryland shade-and-moisture link established for arid agrivoltaics [@barrongafford2019]. The buffering also raises water-use efficiency under shaded pasture [@adeh2018], and modeling reproduces the same soil-moisture response in arid Northwest China [@wu2022]. The crop-facing magnitudes — how much the buffering helps or hurts a given crop — are carried by the shade-tolerance sources in [§5](5-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) and remain **climate- and crop-conditional**. In short: the physics is verified and the dryland benefit well-evidenced, but in temperate and humid settings the effect's sign and size depend on a geometry-and-climate match and stay conditional.

### 4.5 Community & economic function {#sec-fn-community}

The one function that is not about the land, and the [SCALE](#sec-scale) **Communities** domain read as an outcome. The other four ask what the ground can provide. This one asks what the people hosting the project actually get. It is the result that the [social-license pressure](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) and the [community-benefit lever](5-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) are aiming at, not another name for them. Three things sit inside it: **economic prosperity** — durable local income and tax base; **livability** — whether people can live alongside the thing and had a real say in it; and **health & equity** — whether the burdens and the benefits land on the same people.

**Mechanism.** A project returns value to its host in several currencies at once: lease and royalty income to the landowner, PILOT and tax revenue to the jurisdiction, wages to local trades through build and O&M, subscription savings to community-solar members, and — where ownership is structured for it — an equity stake rather than only a rent. Diversified income can be the difference that keeps a marginal farm solvent — the organizing logic of [marginal land solar](6-archetypes.qmd#arch-marginal). The livability and equity sub-capacities turn less on the size of the payment than on the *procedure*: engagement early enough to shape the design, and a distribution of benefit and burden the community reads as fair. This is why benefit and acceptance come apart — a check without a fair process reads as a bribe (§3.1).

**Whose benefit — the actors do not move together.** "The community" is not one party, and a benefit to one can be a loss to another, so this function is only legible once the recipients are named separately:

- **Landowner** — lease and royalty income; the party a land payment reaches first, and often the only one it reaches.
- **Tenant farmer** — frequently the party who *loses*. Nearly 40% of agricultural land in California's Central Valley is rented or leased, and the leading analysis of agrisolar economics there assumes returns reach landowning or partial-owning farmers — naming that assumption as one of its own limitations [@stid2025]. A conversion that sustains an owner can end the operation of the person actually farming the ground. This is the sharpest misalignment in the set, and the one a lease-income argument most often hides.
- **Farm operation and succession** — whether the enterprise itself survives, which is the test [S3 coexistence](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) applies.
- **Neighboring residents** — bear viewshed, construction traffic, and glare, usually without a payment; the party [screening](5-terminology.qmd#term-screening) and good-neighbor agreements address.
- **Local government** — PILOT and tax base, against service and road costs.
- **Tribal nations and communities of place** — treaty rights, cultural landscapes, and consultation standing that do not reduce to a payment.
- **Workers** — construction and O&M wages, and whether they are local and durable rather than transient.
- **Subscribers and ratepayers** — community-solar savings, which may accrue well outside the host community entirely.

A project can score well on one of these and badly on the rest. Naming them separately is what keeps "community benefit" from collapsing into "somebody was paid."

**Design dependencies.** The institutional levers are primary — ownership and control structure, offtake structure, and the [community-benefit](5-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) instruments (CBA / HCA, PILOT, good-neighbor payments, community-solar subscription, local hiring, co-ownership). [Screening](5-terminology.qmd#term-screening) and edge treatment carry the livability sub-capacity on the visual side. Unlike the biophysical functions this one is not much bounded by scale zone or sharing position — it is reachable across the transect — but its *character* shifts with scale: a farmstead array serves one household's resilience, a utility array a jurisdiction's tax base.

**Where on the map.** Reachable at every position, because every project has a host — but its dominant currency changes along the transect. At the farmstead and small-parcel end it is private economic resilience; at utility scale it is fiscal base, local hiring, and subscriber access. It is most at risk where a project is developer-owned, absentee, and offers benefit without engagement; most fully realized under locally-owned or co-ownership models with early, genuine participation.

**Evidence status.** The design principle is **verified** in the ecovoltaic frameworks themselves: @tolgyesi2023 make stakeholder engagement embedded in a viable business model one of five co-equal design pillars — treating community and economic viability as a design question, not an afterthought. The burden side is better measured: interviews on who gains and who bears the costs [@bessette2024], and property-value effects near arrays across six US states [@elmallah2023]. The benefit mechanisms — lease income, PILOT and tax revenue, community-solar savings, local jobs — are real and documented, but largely in **gray literature** (developer disclosures, NREL economic-impact tooling, community-benefit guidance) rather than a settled peer-reviewed synthesis; the grazing-economics and community-benefit sources are recorded as *trace before citing* in the [Sources](sources.qmd). In short: the function is real and widely practiced, its instruments well known, but which structures deliver durable, fairly-shared benefit is still thinly evidenced.
